item.title: Election 2026: Tiburon Town Council candidates differ on parks funding, term limits, Flock, AI
item.description: Tiburon Town Council candidates split on private park money, term limits and AI in follow-up interviews, but all five were open to a hearing on Flock cameras.
item.content:encoded:
Tiburon Town Council candidates differed on private money for parks, term limits and artificial intelligence in follow-up interviews with The Ark, though all five said they were open to a public hearing on the town’s Flock license-plate cameras.

Kathleen Defever, Alice Fredericks, Chuck Hornbrook, Faris Jafar and Jack Ryan answered questions over the past two weeks that the Sept. 29 candidate forum, hosted by The Ark and moderated by the League of Women Voters of Marin County, did not have time to reach.

Defever, Hornbrook and Jafar are each seeking their first term on the council. Ryan, on the council since winning a 2020 special election, is seeking his second full term, while Fredericks is seeking a seventh term after being first elected in 2001.

Election 2026: Read complete coverage at thearknewspaper.com/election2026

The five candidates are vying for three seats in the Nov. 3 election. The winners will serve four-year terms that end November 2030.

At the candidate forum, candidates mostly agreed that residents should help oversee town finances but were split on the town’s use of Flock license-plate cameras, housing approaches and paying for parks.

The follow-up interviews also covered which park projects to build first, community resiliency, term limits, artificial intelligence and civic engagement.

Candidates differ on private money for parks

Candidates differed on seeking private contributions for the parks on top of public money and on how to decide what gets built if the town cannot afford every project at once.

Total costs for the revamped Bel Aire play area, which is under construction, are estimated at $1.02 million, and the projected construction cost of a park at the former sanitation ponds site near McKegney Green has climbed to $3.7 million. Town officials are also scaling back a redesign of Cypress Hollow Park, aiming to cut its $2.5 million price tag at least in half.

The next council will also have to decide how to proceed if the planned projects together prove too expensive. The town has not decided how to pay for the ponds park, and the earliest voters could approve a tax or bond for it is November 2028.

Ryan said it was “perfectly reasonable” to explore how to obtain funding, including community contributions, but he said he wanted to “move forward absent those.”

item.title: Resident group says Belvedere issued Mallard Pointe permits prematurely
item.description: Belvedere Residents for Intelligent Growth has appealed Mallard Pointe bulkhead permits; the City Council will hear the appeal Nov. 9, and work continues meanwhile.
item.content:encoded:
Belvedere Residents for Intelligent Growth has appealed the city’s Mallard Pointe bulkhead permits, arguing they were issued before required geotechnical and flood-plain reviews were done. The city has said it can’t halt work while the appeal waits for a City Council hearing.

The group, formed in 2021 to fight the 40-home redevelopment, filed the appeal Oct. 6, five days after the city issued the two permits for tearing out and replacing the shoreline bulkhead along the Belvedere Lagoon edge of the 1-22 Mallard Road site. It asks the council to rescind or suspend the permits and stop bulkhead work until the steps it says are missing are done.

The council will hear the appeal Nov. 9, or earlier if possible, the city said in an Oct. 12 update to residents.

In an Oct. 9 letter to the group’s attorney, City Manager Robert Zadnik said the city could not grant the request to stop work in the meantime. Under the state building code the city has adopted, the building official may suspend a permit only if it was “issued in error or on the basis of incorrect, inaccurate or incomplete information, or in violation of any ordinance or regulation,” Zadnik said, citing the code, and an appeal alone is not grounds.

“The building official does not believe that any of these circumstances apply in the instant case,” he said.
item.dc:creator: Kevin Hessel

item.title: Belvedere resident sues Tiburon, police officers over alleged wrongful arrest, privacy violations
item.description: A Belvedere resident is suing Tiburon and three police officers, alleging an arrest without probable cause on an October 2025 domestic-violence call.
item.content:encoded:
A Belvedere resident is suing the town of Tiburon and three police officers, saying officers arrested her without probable cause on a domestic-violence call in October 2025 and refused to let her dress before taking her to jail.

Veronika Van Den Top, who lived in Tiburon at the time of her arrest, filed the civil suit Sept. 22 in Marin County Superior Court and is seeking a jury trial. She alleges that police Sgt. Freddy Gutierrez and Officer James Harris violated her civil rights by arresting her without probable cause.

The Marin County District Attorney’s Office did not file a criminal complaint over the arrest, said Alfiya Nachtigall, an administrative secretary for the office.

In a separate family-court case, a Superior Court judge denied requests by Van Den Top and her husband for longer-term domestic-violence restraining orders against each other Feb. 27 after a contested hearing, court records show.
item.dc:creator: Francisco Martinez

item.title: Election 2026: Assembly Democrats Lucan, Elward agree on policy, spar over outside money
item.description: Assembly candidates Eric Lucan and Jackie Elward agreed on most policy at a Sept. 30 forum but sparred over millions in outside money in the 12th District race.
item.content:encoded:
The two Democrats competing to succeed Assemblymember Damon Connolly agreed on most policy questions at an online candidate forum, but Marin Supervisor Eric Lucan and Rohnert Park Councilmember Jackie Elward sparred over the millions in outside money flooding their race.

The Sept. 30 webinar was hosted by the Coalition of Sensible Taxpayers, a Marin taxpayer-advocacy group, and moderated by Marin Independent Journal columnist Dick Spotswood.

Both candidates said they support state funding to finish high-speed rail, oppose Proposition 43, which would make local tax measures put on the ballot by citizen initiative harder to pass, and would have backed a police and firefighter pension bill Gov. Gavin Newsom vetoed last month. Lucan’s answers centered on financing tools for housing, Elward’s on local control and accountability for state spending.

Election 2026: Read complete coverage at thearknewspaper.com/election2026

The 12th Assembly District covers all of Marin County and part of Sonoma County, including Rohnert Park and a portion of Petaluma. Connolly, D-San Rafael, is running for the state Senate seat being vacated by Sen. Mike McGuire, who is termed out.

Lucan, a former three-term Novato councilmember and mayor elected to the Board of Supervisors in 2022, led the six-candidate June 2 primary with 28.3%. Elward, a former Rohnert Park mayor and an educator who came to the U.S. from the Democratic Republic of Congo, was second at 22.6%. Under California’s top-two system, the two highest vote-getters advance regardless of party.

Tiburon Councilmember Holli Thier, the only candidate from the peninsula, finished fourth at 14% and conceded in June. Lucan led on the Tiburon Peninsula in early returns, with 28.7% of the 4,712 votes counted at the time, ahead of Thier at 23.6%.

A fight over who is paying

Spotswood asked each candidate how big money would affect their decisions in Sacramento. He said Lucan had received $551,000 in September from Grow California, a political action committee founded by tech and cryptocurrency billionaires Tim Draper and Chris Larsen.

Lucan said that was wrong.

“I did not receive that contribution, and I have not received any money from that group. Those are independent expenditures that are happening completely without my knowledge,” he said.

item.title: Election 2026: State Senate candidates Connolly, Gibbs clash over taxes, housing, homelessness
item.description: State Senate candidates Damon Connolly and Tief Gibbs split over Marin’s childcare tax, homelessness and a statewide tax measure, but both vowed to rein in state housing laws.
item.content:encoded:
The two Marin residents vying to succeed termed-out state Sen. Mike McGuire split over Marin’s childcare parcel tax, homelessness and a statewide measure to make citizen-initiated local taxes harder to pass, though both pledged to rein in state housing laws.

Assemblymember Damon Connolly, D-San Rafael, and Republican Tief Gibbs of Novato answered questions for more than an hour Sept. 24 in an online forum hosted by the Coalition of Sensible Taxpayers, a Marin taxpayer-advocacy group Connolly thanked for endorsing him in his 2022 Assembly race. Marin Independent Journal columnist Dick Spotswood moderated.

The 2nd State Senate District, which includes the Tiburon Peninsula, runs from the Golden Gate Bridge to the Oregon border, taking in Del Norte, Humboldt, Lake, Marin, Mendocino and Trinity counties and part of Sonoma. McGuire, a Democrat and former Senate president pro tem, is running for Congress in the 1st District.

Election 2026: Read complete coverage at thearknewspaper.com/election2026

Both would loosen state housing rules

Both candidates said they would roll back or rewrite state housing laws that override local zoning.

Connolly is a former Marin supervisor, San Rafael councilmember and state deputy attorney general who has represented Marin in the Assembly since 2022. He said he had not supported Senate Bill 79, the 2025 law that took effect July 1 and allows apartment buildings of five to nine stories within a half-mile of major transit stations in urban counties, or Assembly Bill 130 and Senate Bill 131, 2025 budget bills that loosened state environmental review for infill housing. He voted against SB 79 and did not vote on final passage of AB 130 or SB 131. All three became law.

He also took aim at the regional housing needs allocation, the state process that sets how many homes each city and county must plan for, saying it assigns numbers within deadlines “that don’t really make sense.” He said the idea of revisiting it has met “a chilly reception so far” among his colleagues.

item.title: Tiburon faces $1.6 million annual gap in road maintenance funding
item.description: Tiburon has about five years of dedicated pavement money left before it would need roughly $1.6 million a year from its general fund to keep up road work.
item.content:encoded:
Tiburon has five years’ worth of funding left for pavement-focused projects before it must dip into its general fund to keep up the same level of maintenance, according to one town official.

Public Works Operations & Technology Manager Patrick Kerslake gave the update Oct. 7 in a “State of the Pavement” presentation to the Town Council. He said the town could need about $1.6 million a year from its general fund to keep spending at current levels once its restricted road reserves run out.

“Basically, the trend reflects a structural funding gap between the town’s desired pavement investment and condition level, and the amount supported by recurring restricted transportation revenues,” Kerslake said.
item.dc:creator: Francisco Martinez
item.media:description: Cracks run across the pavement of Reedland Woods Way in Tiburon on Oct. 7. The town intends to repave the street next summer, and resident Tim Metz said town staff told him it scores 41 out of 100 on the pavement-condition index. (Francisco Martinez / The Ark)

item.title: Belvedere may seek more time for Beach Road seawall work
item.description: Belvedere’s Beach Road seawall work will likely run into November, and the city may seek an extension past its Oct. 30 deadline for in-water work.
item.content:encoded:
Construction on Belvedere’s Beach Road stabilization project will likely continue into November, with city officials anticipating they may need an extension to complete work in the water beyond an Oct. 30 deadline.

Public Works Director Antony Boyd told the Beach Road Stabilization Project Oversight Subcommittee on Oct. 7 that crews have begun installing 42-foot steel sheet piles along the shoreline. The contractor has revised the construction sequence to finish as much in-water work as possible before returning to the street-side portion of the project.

“There have been delays, and it definitely looks like it will be going into November to complete the work,” Boyd said. Finishing the in-water work by Oct. 30 remains “quite tight,” he added.

The city expects to decide whether to seek an extension in the last two weeks before the deadline, when weather forecasts and the amount of remaining work will be clearer.
item.dc:creator: Tyler Callister
item.media:description: A crane lifts a steel sheet pile along Beach Road in Belvedere the afternoon of Oct. 6, as crews reinforce about 550 feet of seawall. Engineers have said the eroding wall could fail in a major earthquake and flood hundreds of lagoon-area homes. (Tyler Callister / The Ark)

item.title: Redesign brings Belvedere’s Artist’s View deck bid under budget
item.description: After first-round bids came in over budget, Belvedere swapped steel for wood in its Artist’s View lookout platform and on Oct. 12 awarded a $172,200 contract.
item.content:encoded:
After every bid in its first round came in over budget, Belvedere swapped much of the steel in its Artist’s View lookout platform for wood and awarded a $172,200 contract on the second try.

The City Council voted unanimously Oct. 12 to give the job to Modernscapes Innovations Inc. It approved the contract without discussion on its consent calendar, which is reserved for items considered routine. The council also authorized a $17,000 contingency for change orders, bringing the total construction authorization to $189,200.

Modernscapes’ bid was the lowest of three opened Sept. 30. Pridex Construction Group bid $220,000 and MARC Builders LLC bid $217,513, according to the city’s bid tabulation. The city engineer’s estimate was $150,000.

Public Works Director Antony Boyd told the city’s Parks, Open Spaces and Lanes Committee on Sept. 17 that the first request for bids, posted in July, drew what he recalled as four bids.

“Unfortunately, they were all above our budget, significantly above the city’s budget for that project,” he said.
item.dc:creator: Tyler Callister
item.media:description: A sketch by Tiburon landscape architect Christianna Seidel shows the viewing platform planned for Artist’s View, a city-owned open-space parcel at the southern tip of Belvedere Island. The city has since revised the platform’s structure to use more wood and less steel to cut costs. (Christianna Seidel via city of Belvedere)

item.title: Belvedere’s Community Park well bid comes in $44,000 over budget
item.description: Belvedere’s only proposal to drill a new well for Community Park irrigation came in at $122,127, about $44,000 over the city’s $78,000 budget.
item.content:encoded:
Belvedere is still looking for a way to replace the aging well that fills Community Park’s irrigation tank after the only proposal to drill a new one came in about $44,000 over budget.

The proposal came from Gordian, a company that supplies public agencies with contractors already vetted under state public-bidding law, and was submitted through the purchasing cooperative Sourcewell. It came to $122,127, against the city’s $78,000 budget for the well, Public Works Director Antony Boyd said in an Oct. 9 email to The Ark. The city will instead run an informal bidding process for the same work, with completion now expected in spring 2027.

Boyd had told the city’s Parks, Open Spaces and Lanes Committee on Sept. 17 that hiring through Gordian would make it easier for the city to get jobs done than a conventional bid.

The city leases the current well on private property near Laurel and Bayview avenues, City Manager Robert Zadnik told The Ark.

“The well has been having production issues, despite our work to try and get it to clean it and maintain it,” he said. “So we’re looking for an alternative. We’re still actively looking to drill a new well somewhere, hopefully in Community Park, to supplement that irrigation water.”
item.dc:creator: Tyler Callister
item.media:description: A wooden tank that is part of Belvedere Community Park’s well system stands near the park’s edge Oct. 7. A contractor’s proposal to drill a new well for the park came in over the city’s budget, and the city is not moving forward with it, Public Works Director Antony Boyd said. (Kevin Hessel / The Ark)

item.title: The Caviar Co. will close Tiburon’s Main Street tasting room Oct. 18 after five years
item.description: The Caviar Co. will close its Main Street tasting room in Tiburon after service Oct. 18; local delivery and online orders continue.
item.content:encoded:
The Caviar Co. will close its Tiburon tasting room at 46A Main St. after service Oct. 18, ending a run of more than five years on lower Main Street.

The tasting room will be open one more weekend: noon-7 p.m. Oct. 16 and 17 and noon-6 p.m. 18, according to the company’s Instagram post.

Owner Petra Higby of Belvedere said in an email that the shop will serve hot dogs and other treats that weekend as a thank-you, will honor all reservations and will welcome walk-ins.

After the closing the company’s local delivery will continue, and caviar can still be ordered online at thecaviarco.com, the post said.
item.dc:creator: Kevin Hessel

item.title: Student art shows bring Reed Union School District classrooms to Tiburon Town Hall
item.description: Reed and Bel Aire students’ artwork goes on view Oct. 19-Nov. 20 at Tiburon Town Hall, the first of two shows, with Del Mar’s advanced students to follow.
item.content:encoded:
Artwork by Reed Union School District students goes on display Oct. 19 at Tiburon Town Hall in the first of two student shows organized by district visual and performing arts teacher Abby O’Leary.

O’Leary, who has taught in the district for more than 30 years, became its visual and performing arts teacher-on-assignment last school year, a position the district created with state Proposition 28 arts and music funding. She works across the district’s three schools: Reed and Bel Aire elementary schools and Del Mar Middle School. She admired how Mill Valley promoted its school district students’ artwork with public exhibits and decided to try the same for the Reed district.

“We need to create stronger ties with our community, with the local residents to see what is happening in our schools,” she said. “Their taxes, after all, are paying for what goes on in the schools, and I think they should know about all the good things that are happening that they might not otherwise know about.”

Knowing weather can spoil an outdoor exhibit, O’Leary wanted the show indoors. She presented her plan to the Tiburon Heritage & Arts Commission, which approved the two-part exhibit.

The Reed and Bel Aire Fall Art Show runs Oct. 19-Nov. 20 in the lower gallery at Tiburon Town Hall, with an opening reception 5:30-7 p.m. Oct. 20. The Del Mar advanced student art show runs Nov. 24-Dec. 22, with a reception 6-8 p.m. Dec. 1. Both shows are free and open to the public during Town Hall hours.
item.dc:creator: Diane Smith
item.media:description: A Bel Aire Elementary School fourth grader drew this fall leaf in oil pastels, using the color wheel’s complementary colors to make it stand out, while ‘Blue Ridge Mountains,’ a watercolor-and-salt painting by a Bel Aire fifth grader, was inspired by John Denver’s ‘Take Me Home, Country Roads.’ They are among the Reed and Bel Aire student works on view Oct. 19-Nov. 20 at Tiburon Town Hall.

item.title: Everyday Encounters: A writer and a filmmaker diagnose the creative life on Tiburon’s Old Rail Trail
item.description: On the Old Rail Trail in Tiburon, aspiring writer Jenna Smith and filmmaker Octavio Kaufman, grandson of director Philip Kaufman, talk about the creative life.
item.content:encoded:
Jenna Smith and her boyfriend, Octavio Kaufman, are walking the Tiburon bike path along Richardson Bay on a brisk morning Oct. 9 when she offers her diagnosis of the creative life.

“It’s a disease,” she says. “We’re too thoughtful and introspective.”

Both are 26, and both spend a lot of time looking within. Smith, a San Francisco resident, is an aspiring writer between jobs — “extremely fun-employed,” she says. Kaufman is a third-generation filmmaker.
item.dc:creator: Tyler Callister
item.media:description: Jenna Smith of San Francisco and her boyfriend, Octavio Kaufman, stop along the Tiburon bike path on Oct. 9. Smith writes a humorous Substack, and Kaufman, whose grandfather directed ‘The Right Stuff,’ makes films and develops scripts. (Tyler Callister / The Ark)

item.title: Mark Hapgood Stiefel
item.description: Mark Hapgood Stiefel passed away on September 28, 2026.
item.content:encoded:
Mark Hapgood Stiefel of Winchester, California, passed away on September 28, 2026, at the age of 79. He was a dairyman, a sailor, and above all, the heart of a big and loving family.

Mark was born on June 11, 1947, and grew up in Artesia, California, when it was still dairy country. He studied dairy science at Cal Poly San Luis Obispo, graduating in 1969. After college, he came home to the work that would be his life’s calling.

As Southern California’s dairies moved east, Mark moved with them, first from Artesia to Chino. In 1989, he built a new dairy from the ground up in Winchester. Stiefel Dairy on Holland Road was his life’s work. Cows don’t take days off, and neither did Mark. He worked seven days a week, year after year, taking great pride in his work and in doing things the right way.

Mark worked hard, but he also knew how to enjoy life. He loved the ocean, and some of his happiest days were spent at the beach or under sail. He sailed to Catalina and raced down the coast to Ensenada with his brother, Mike. Those adventures and memories were a special part of who he was.

He was also a self-trained chef and really enjoyed experimenting in the kitchen. Beware of the infamous Troubadour beans!

Above all, Mark loved his family. He was a devoted father and a fun, deeply loving grandfather. He had a gift for bringing people together and made it a priority to keep family members connected to one another. That may be his greatest legacy: a family that knows and loves each other because he saw to it.

He was preceded in death by his wife, Catherine Stiefel on July 23, 2018.

Mark is survived by his children, Julie Kusiak, Marcia Stiefel, Jack and Alison Stiefel (of Tiburon) and Matt Stiefel and his brother, Mike Stiefel. He is also survived by his beloved grandchildren, Tyler Mason, Ricquel Crouse, Ava Miller, Troy Stiefel, Elise Stiefel, Sofie Stiefel and Simone Stiefel (also of Tiburon), a large and loving extended family, and many wonderful lifelong friends.

Fair winds and following seas, Mark. You are deeply loved, and you will be deeply missed. The memories you gave us, the hard work, the laughter, the off-road adventures, and most of all the love you had for your family will live on forever in all of us.

A Celebration of Life will be announced later this year.

item.title: Election 2026: Tam Union board member Kevin Saavedra resigns day after restraining order, stays on ballot
item.description: Tamalpais Union High School District board member Kevin Saavedra resigned Oct. 9, a day after a judge’s restraining order, but stays on the Nov. 3 ballot.
item.content:encoded:
Tamalpais Union High School District board member Kevin Saavedra resigned Oct. 9, a day after a judge ordered him to stay away from a district parent he had cursed at in emails — yet he stays on the Nov. 3 ballot for a third term.

Saavedra, the board’s clerk, quit in a letter emailed that Friday to Superintendent Courtney Goode and board President Cynthia Roenisch, effective immediately, the Redwood Bark, Redwood High’s student newspaper, first reported. The letter does not mention the court order or name anyone.

“The most recent cycle has been tumultuous,” Saavedra wrote. “In service of this volunteer position I would not have expected I would be told I am to withstand personal and sometimes racist attacks. Or doxing. Or stalking. The abuse has been draining and I have had enough.”

Election 2026: Read complete coverage at thearknewspaper.com/election2026

He told the Bark he “would not bet” on taking the seat if he is reelected.

Also Oct. 9 the district announced that Roenisch had proposed censuring Saavedra “for his unprofessional and aggressive communications directed toward a district parent.” The motion is on the board’s 6 p.m. Oct. 13 agenda. Whether it would go forward was not known at The Ark’s press deadline.

The five-member board governs Redwood High in Larkspur, which most Tiburon Peninsula high schoolers attend.

Marin County Superior Court Judge Mark A. Talamantes granted the three-year civil harassment restraining order Oct. 8, barring Saavedra, 55, from any contact with Ina Gotlieb, a 56-year-old college admissions counselor, or her child, a student at one of the district’s two alternative high schools.

Gotlieb petitioned Sept. 28, citing some 10 months of emails and videos from Saavedra.

The dispute began last November at a board meeting on putting the Tamiscal and San Andreas alternative schools on one campus, where Roenisch held dozens of speakers, many of them students, to one minute each. That night Gotlieb emailed Roenisch, calling her an expletive and a “sad old woman.” Roenisch did not reply but forwarded the email to Saavedra. Gotlieb later apologized to Roenisch.

Saavedra then emailed Gotlieb from his district account, telling her to “go f— yourself you stupid old crone.” More emails followed, including one from his campaign account and another saying he was asking her neighbors about her, along with YouTube videos criticizing her.

item.title: Ex-SFPD sergeant kills wife, a former deputy chief, and daughter in Strawberry murder-suicide
item.description: A retired San Francisco police sergeant shot and killed his wife, a former deputy chief, and their 24-year-old daughter in Strawberry, then himself, the Sheriff’s Office said.
item.content:encoded:
A retired San Francisco police sergeant shot and killed his wife, a former deputy chief, and their 24-year-old daughter in their Strawberry home Oct. 11, then killed himself, according to the Marin County Sheriff’s Office.

The office identified them Oct. 12 as Kevin Mannix, 68; Ann Mannix, 65; and Katherine “Katie” Mannix. Its findings are preliminary. The office has not said what led to the shooting.

Dispatchers received a 911 call at 5:03 p.m. The couple’s other daughter, who had been in the home and got out, made the call, The Ark confirmed independently.

She told dispatchers that her father had shot her mother and sister with a handgun, that she had heard six to nine shots and that she had locked herself in a bedroom, according to recorded emergency radio traffic. An automated fall-detection alert from an Apple Watch at the home, with no one speaking on the line, also reached dispatchers.

Deputies arrived a few minutes later, set up a perimeter and went inside to make sure no threat remained, Miguel Almaguer, the office’s public information officer, said at a news conference at the scene that night.

The daughter came out of the house with her hands raised before deputies went in, according to the radio traffic. Deputies found the three inside, with a handgun next to Kevin Mannix, the radio traffic shows.

The surviving daughter’s husband also called 911, and several neighbors called to report hearing gunshots, according to the radio traffic. Deputies interviewed witnesses at nearby homes on Strawberry Circle that night.

There appeared to be no earlier calls for service at the address, Almaguer said that night. Investigators and the county coroner finished processing the scene by Oct. 12, and autopsies were scheduled for Oct. 13, according to the Sheriff’s Office.

“There is no threat to the community,” Almaguer said.

San Francisco Police Chief Derrick Lew told department members of the couple’s deaths in a 7:37 p.m. email that night, which The Ark obtained.

“It is with heavy hearts that we share the news of the passing of Ann and Kevin Mannix,” Lew said in the email. “Please keep their family in your prayers.”

The deaths have “left our entire SFPD family reeling,” Louis Wong, president of the San Francisco Police Officers Association, said in a statement Oct. 12.

item.title: Election 2026: Tiburon Town Council hopefuls talk traffic, finances, housing at Ark forum
item.description: Tiburon Town Council candidates mostly agreed at a Sept. 29 forum that residents should help oversee town finances but split on Flock cameras, housing sites and park funding.
item.content:encoded:
Tiburon Town Council candidates mostly agreed at a Sept. 29 forum that residents should help oversee town finances but split on Flock cameras, housing sites and paying for parks.

More than 50 people packed Town Hall’s council chambers and nearly 150 people tuned in on The Ark’s Instagram page for the forum, hosted by The Ark and moderated by the League of Women Voters of Marin County, to hear from incumbents Alice Fredericks and Jack Ryan and challengers Kathleen Defever, Chuck Hornbrook and Faris Jafar. The top three vote-getters in the Nov. 3 election will win four-year terms that end November 2030.

Defever, 48, is a lawyer who has served since 2018 on the Planning Commission and is seeking her first term on the council.

Election 2026: Read complete coverage at thearknewspaper.com/election2026

In her opening statement, she pointed to her expertise in insurance and her work representing fire victims, saying the denser housing the town must plan for under its housing element, which requires sites for 639 units by 2031, would add to fire risk on the peninsula.

“I am the person most equipped to handle those questions and to come up with constructive solutions,” Defever said.

Fredericks, 86, is a former behavioral-medicine researcher at the University of California at San Francisco who is the longest-serving councilmember in Tiburon’s history and has served as mayor on five occasions. She’s seeking a seventh term after being first elected in 2001.

She pointed to her work representing the town on countywide agencies, such as the Transportation Authority of Marin, and on county sea-level-rise planning committees.

“My work in the last few years has focused on community and government bodies that foster collaboration and coordination — and please don’t go to sleep, because in this day and age, it’s very important,” Fredericks said.

She also said the town is not done with park improvements, floating the idea of acquiring the Richardson Bay Sanitary District’s remaining land for a community center.

Hornbrook, 59, is a part-time adviser to clean-energy companies and a member of the Parks, Open Space & Trails Commission.

item.title: Tiburon sanitary district considers overhaul of odor-control system
item.description: Sanitary District No. 5 of Marin is weighing $1 million to $11 million fixes for the 21-year-old odor-control system at its Paradise Drive plant in Tiburon.
item.content:encoded:
Jim Miller said his Centro West Street home might have the best view in town, if not the world. This year, he said, it has also come with the smell of the sewage plant on Paradise Drive.

Sanitary District No. 5 of Marin, which runs the plant, is weighing what to do about the 21-year-old system meant to contain the odor. Its choices run from $1 million to $2 million to rehabilitate the equipment to roughly $11 million over 20 years to replace it.

The district’s board voted unanimously Sept. 17 to accept the Carollo Engineers report laying out the options and directed District Manager Tony Rubio to work with the district’s capital improvement program committee on budgeting and implementation. Rubio’s staff report recommended that the work focus on rehabilitating the current system. No project, budget or construction timeline has been approved.

“We’ve got an odor-control system that works, but with any big project, you have to prioritize funding — how much and how fast,” Rubio said. “It goes back to committee for figuring out all those loose ends.”

item.title: Election 2026: Tamalpais Union board hopefuls split over trust, budget at forum
item.description: Seven candidates for three Tamalpais Union High School District board seats split over whether the board has lost community trust, at a Sept. 28 forum in Larkspur.
item.content:encoded:
Two incumbents and five challengers vying for three Tamalpais Union High School District board seats are divided over whether the board has lost the community’s trust after a year of contested votes on support programs for Black students, cellphones and the district’s alternative schools.

Six of the seven candidates made their cases Sept. 28 at a League of Women Voters of Marin County forum at the Kreps Conference Center in Larkspur, co-hosted by Marin Promise Partnership. Challenger Maria Sandoval, a Mill Valley resident who teaches Spanish at a San Francisco private school and serves on the Marin County Free Library Commission, did not attend. In her League of Women Voters guide answers, she listed rebuilding trust through listening and collaboration as her first priority.

The district runs Redwood High School, the main public high school for Tiburon and Belvedere students, and Tamalpais High School, which serves Strawberry, along with Archie Williams High School in San Anselmo and two alternative schools. Board members are elected districtwide.

Election 2026: Read complete coverage at thearknewspaper.com/election2026

The two incumbents on the ballot, board President Cynthia Roenisch and Kevin Saavedra, cast the race as a question of experience, arguing the district has steadied its finances and raised test scores under Superintendent Courtney Goode and needs seasoned board members through a tightening budget. Most of the challengers said the board must first rebuild trust with students, parents and teachers.

The third seat is open because board member Emily Uhlhorn chose not to seek reelection. She will finish her term and become executive director of the Tam High Foundation in January.

Roenisch, a Corte Madera resident who teaches Advanced Placement English at Alameda High School and is a former litigator, served on the Kentfield School District board before joining the Tam board and led the search that hired Goode. Saavedra, of San Anselmo, described his background as private equity and investment banking; his two children graduated from Sir Francis Drake High, now Archie Williams. He is the only candidate who did not file a statement for the county voter guide.

The moderator, reading from questions submitted by the public, prefaced one by citing “significant discord between the district and the community,” evidenced by contentious board meetings.

item.title: Election 2026: Open governor’s race, billionaire tax top California ballot
item.description: Peninsula ballots carry an open California governor’s race, 14 state propositions including a one-time billionaire tax, and an open Assembly seat.
item.content:encoded:
Ballots arriving in peninsula mailboxes this week carry an open governor’s race, 14 statewide propositions — among them a one-time 5% tax on billionaires and two competing measures that would cancel it — and an Assembly seat that two Democrats are vying to fill.

Marin County elections officials began mailing ballots to every active registered voter by Oct. 5. The last day to register is Oct. 19, though voters can still register and vote at a vote center or the county elections office through Election Day, Nov. 3, when polls are open 7 a.m.-8 p.m.

The Ark has covered the local races and measures on peninsula ballots in separate stories. This roundup covers the state and federal contests: the offices first, then the propositions. Each of the 14 propositions needs a simple majority to pass.

Election 2026: Read complete coverage at thearknewspaper.com/election2026

Governor: Becerra vs. Hilton

State official, all voters

Gov. Gavin Newsom is termed out, and the race to succeed him pits Democrat Xavier Becerra, a former U.S. Health and Human Services secretary, California attorney general and longtime Los Angeles-area congressman, against Republican Steve Hilton of Atherton, a former Fox News host and onetime senior adviser to British Prime Minister David Cameron.

Becerra led the June 2 primary statewide with 28%, ahead of Hilton’s 24.6%. In Marin, Becerra ran second to Democrat Tom Steyer, who did not advance, while Hilton drew 14.2%. A Republican hasn’t won the governor’s office since 2006.

Becerra has pledged to declare a state of emergency to fund 40,000 already-approved affordable homes and to fully fund the court-ordered drug treatment created by Proposition 36, the 2024 measure that stiffened penalties for some drug and theft crimes. He would also use emergency powers to freeze utility rates and crack down on price gouging. Hilton, endorsed by President Donald Trump, would eliminate state income tax on the first $150,000 of earnings and set a flat rate above that, halve the gas tax, roll back greenhouse gas and renewable-energy mandates, ban street camping outright and repeal the state’s sanctuary law.

item.title: Reed school district inclusion efforts filmed for documentary series
item.description: A crew for Andy Garcia’s public-television docuseries filmed Reed Union School District classrooms Sept. 24 for a segment on including students with disabilities.
item.content:encoded:
A film crew for a public-television docuseries hosted by actor Andy Garcia spent Sept. 24 in Reed Union School District classrooms, recording how the district includes students with disabilities.

The segment, “Breaking Down Barriers for Neurodivergent Learners,” is set to air on “All Access with Andy Garcia,” a short-form series that runs between longer programs on public-television stations nationwide. Garcia is known for roles in “Ocean’s Eleven” and “The Godfather Part III.”

Documentarians filmed interviews with district officials inside an unused Del Mar Middle School classroom and captured classroom footage there as well as at Reed and Bel Aire elementary schools. The segment is scheduled for release before the end of the year.

The district board approved the filming agreement without discussion Sept. 15. It barred filming any student in an identifiable way without a parent’s signed consent, cost the district nothing and gives the district a chance to review footage of its students and staff before broadcast.
